findings.claim: At paragraph 13, John Paul II reflects on how suffering occupies a privileged place in the Christian understanding of the world - not because suffering is good in itself, but because Christ transformed it.
findings.truth: Salvifici Doloris 13 opens 'But in order to perceive the true answer to the why of suffering, we must look to the revelation of divine love', and states that love is the fullest source of the answer to the meaning of suffering. The lesson's summary is not what paragraph 13 says. The same wrong summary is repeated in flashcard 10.
findings.evidence: vatican.va, John Paul II, Salvifici Doloris (11 Feb 1984), section 13

findings.claim: Knowledge check 4: 'In the free will defence, God allows the possibility of evil because genuine _____ requires the freedom to choose wrong.' Options: intelligence / faith / freedom / love. Key = index 2 (freedom).
findings.truth: The answer is 'love' (index 3). The lesson text says a world of beings who could only do good 'would not be a world of love, because love requires free choice'. With 'freedom' the sentence is circular, and a student giving the lesson's own answer is marked wrong.
findings.evidence: Recomputation against lesson 1 content_html, free will defence paragraph (n11)

findings.truth: The validator limit is under 100 characters. Shortened to 96.

findings.claim: The 8-mark stems in lessons 1 and 2 end 'Refer to sacred writings or another source of Catholic belief and teaching in your answer.'
findings.truth: That instruction line is another board's question rubric, adapted. This board's 8-mark question asks for sources of wisdom and authority in its own wording, and the house copyright rule forbids reusing a board's question wording. Lesson 3 already uses the house form 'Refer to a source of Catholic teaching in your answer.' Lessons 1 and 2 now match it.
findings.evidence: House copyright-distancing rule in CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md; lesson 3 practice question 5

findings.claim: Jesus Christ is therefore described in the Nicene Creed as 'fully God and fully human'.
findings.truth: The Nicene Creed contains no such phrase. It says 'true God from true God ... and became man'. 'Perfect in Godhead and perfect in manhood ... truly God and truly man' is the Definition of the Council of Chalcedon (451), which the lesson names in the very next sentence. Attributing the quoted phrase to the Creed is a wrong attribution of a named spec source.
findings.evidence: Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed text (Roman Missal 2011); Chalcedonian Definition, 451

findings.claim: The Creed is quoted as 'true God from true God, begotten, not made, of one Being with the Father', and the paragraph states that Catholics recite this Creed at Mass. The same wording appears in flashcard 1 and in two practice mark schemes; one mark scheme also lists 'the only Son of God'.
findings.truth: 'Of one Being with the Father' is the 1975 ICEL/ecumenical rendering. The text Catholics have recited at Mass since Advent 2011 reads 'begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father', and 'the Only Begotten Son of God'. Because the lesson frames the quotation as what is said at Mass, the current Missal wording is the correct one. Four occurrences aligned.
findings.evidence: Roman Missal, third edition (2011), Order of Mass, Nicene Creed; CCC 242 ('consubstantial')

findings.claim: Philippians 2 quoted as Christ 'did not consider equality with God something to be used to his own advantage; rather, he emptied himself by taking the nature of a servant.'
findings.truth: This is a hybrid that matches no translation: the first clause is NIV (2011), but NIV continues 'he made himself nothing by taking the very nature of a servant'. The RSV Catholic Edition reads 'did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant' - which also matches the 'form of a servant' wording used elsewhere in the lesson.
findings.evidence: Philippians 2:6-7, RSV Catholic Edition; compared with NIV (2011) and NRSV

findings.claim: Britain sends one of the largest national pilgrimages to Lourdes each year, organised by the Catholic Bishops' Conference of England and Wales.
findings.truth: The Bishops' Conference of England and Wales does not organise a national Lourdes pilgrimage. Pilgrimages from England and Wales are run by individual dioceses and by Catholic charities (HCPT, the Order of Malta, Across). The lesson's own key fact and conclusion already say this correctly.
findings.evidence: Internal contradiction with the lesson's key fact (HCPT) and conclusion ('British dioceses send large pilgrimage groups')

findings.claim: The sculpture also mediates on the relationship between the Incarnation and redemption.
findings.truth: 'Mediates on' is a word error for 'meditates on', and a sculpture does not meditate. Reworded to 'expresses the relationship'.

findings.claim: Description is 105 characters and spells the sculpture 'Pieta' without its accent.
findings.truth: The validator limit is under 100 characters and the plain-text field takes unicode. Shortened to 94 characters with 'Pieta' corrected to 'Pietà'.
findings.evidence: Character count; house rule that plain-text fields use unicode

findings.claim: The Catechism of the Catholic Church (paragraph 2132) draws a sharp distinction between latria (worship owed to God alone) and dulia (honour given to saints), with a higher form - hyperdulia - reserved for Mary.
findings.truth: CCC 2132 does draw the substantive distinction ('the honor rendered to an image passes to its prototype ... a respectful veneration, not the adoration due to God alone'), but it does not use the Latin terms latria, dulia or hyperdulia; hyperdulia sits nearer CCC 971. Options: (a) leave it - the substance is right and no mark turns on it; (b) reword to 'The Catechism (paragraph 2132) teaches that the honour given to an image passes to the person it represents. Catholic theology distinguishes latria ... from dulia ...'. Recommend (b), but it is a sentence rewrite rather than a fact correction, so it is left for a ruling.
findings.evidence: vatican.va, Catechism of the Catholic Church 2129-2132 and 971
findings.ruling: NOTE: latria/dulia/hyperdulia sentence cites CCC 2132 loosely; the distinction itself is standard Catholic teaching (CCC 971, 2113); left for an authoring pass.

findings.claim: At paragraph 23, he teaches that suffering can become a school of virtue - the occasion for developing patience, compassion, courage and solidarity with those who suffer.
findings.truth: Salvifici Doloris 23 is about suffering as a trial and the gospel paradox of weakness and strength ('power is made perfect in weakness'). 'A school of virtue' is a fair gloss and the spec does list 'the role of suffering in the development of the virtues', but the four named virtues are not in the text. Options: (a) leave the gloss; (b) drop the named list. Recommend (a) - it is spec-aligned and no mark turns on the list.
findings.ruling: NOTE: Salvifici Doloris 23 gloss is spec-aligned; no mark at risk; left.

findings.claim: Scripture quoted in NIV wording inside a Catholic theology unit: Matthew 3:17 'This is my Son, whom I love' (lesson 2) and Romans 8:20-21 creation 'subject to frustration' (lesson 1).
findings.truth: NRSVCE reads 'This is my Son, the Beloved, with whom I am well pleased' and 'the creation was subjected to futility'. Both lesson versions are accurate NIV, so no mark is at risk; a Catholic-approved translation would be more consistent with the rest of the unit.
findings.evidence: Matthew 3:17 and Romans 8:20 in NRSV/NRSVCE compared with NIV

findings.claim: Pope Francis's apostolic exhortation Evangelii Gaudium (2013) acknowledged that popular expressions of faith 'manifest a thirst for God which only the poor and the simple can know.'
findings.truth: The sentence originates with Paul VI, Evangelii Nuntiandi 48 (1975), whose English text reads 'It manifests a thirst for God which only the simple and poor can know.' Evangelii Gaudium quotes it in its section on the evangelising power of popular piety, so the attribution is defensible, but the lesson does not say Francis is quoting Paul VI.

findings.claim: Catholics recite the Nicene Creed at Mass every Sunday ... Recited at every Sunday Mass.
findings.truth: The Apostles' Creed is a permitted alternative at Sunday Mass, especially in Lent and Eastertide and at Masses with children. 'Usually' would be exact; no mark turns on it.
findings.evidence: Roman Missal, third edition, Order of Mass rubric on the Profession of Faith

summary: Three lessons checked against the Route B Component 1 Theme 2 content and the 2/5/8/15 question ladder. Exam framing, tariffs, Trent 1563, the Pieta (c.1499, St Peter's Basilica), Lourdes 1858 and Bernadette's 1933 canonisation, Chalcedon 451, Nicaea 325 / Constantinople 381, Enchiridion 3:11, De Trinitate 8.10, Marialis Cultus 1974, Rosarium Virginis Mariae 2002, CCC 967 and 1521, and every other answer key all check out; no lesson names the board. Two HIGH errors: a knowledge-check key that marks the true answer wrong, and the phrase 'fully God and fully human' attributed to the Nicene Creed rather than to Chalcedon. Ten findings fixed across 15 edits; two left for a ruling.
